explanations.answer: Rise up and rebuild God's house
explanations.explanation: Yes, friend. Zerubbabel son of Shealtiel, a leader of the exiles who came home, and Jeshua son of Jozadak, a priest, “rose up and began to rebuild the house of God in Jerusalem.” (Ezra 5:2) The prophets spoke, and these two got moving. No long meeting first, just work boots on.

Not this time, friend. Zerubbabel son of Shealtiel, a leader of the exiles, and Jeshua son of Jozadak, a priest, did the opposite of leaving. The text says they “rose up and began to rebuild the house of God in Jerusalem.” (Ezra 5:2) Packing a suitcase while the prophets are still echoing would be a bold move.

That's a sensible guess, but the text has them starting first. Zerubbabel son of Shealtiel and Jeshua son of Jozadak “rose up and began to rebuild the house of God in Jerusalem.” (Ezra 5:2) The question about authorization doesn't come up until Tattenai, the governor of the region west of the Euphrates, arrives. So the building was already underway when the questions started.

I can see why you'd think so, but the text says something different. “…the prophets of God were with them, helping them.” (Ezra 5:2) Haggai and Zechariah didn't hand over a pile of stones and wish the builders luck. They stayed right there with them.

That's it, baker. The text says the prophets of God were with Zerubbabel and Jeshua, helping them. (Ezra 5:2) It doesn't spell out how they helped, but they were right there in the work. I think a builder feels braver with a prophet at his elbow.

You got it, baker. Tattenai, the governor of the region west of the Euphrates, asks, “Who authorized you to rebuild this temple and restore this structure?” (Ezra 5:3) That's the big question of the whole passage. He wants to know who gave the okay.

explanations.answer: How much the building will cost
explanations.explanation: Good thinking, since any governor would care about a budget. But the text never has Tattenai ask about money. His question is, “Who authorized you to rebuild this temple and restore this structure?” (Ezra 5:3) He wants to know who gave the okay, not what it costs.

explanations.answer: When the building will be finished
explanations.explanation: That's a fair thing for a governor to wonder, but it isn't what he asks. Tattenai asks, “Who authorized you to rebuild this temple and restore this structure?” (Ezra 5:3) Nobody's checking a calendar here. He's checking who gave the okay.
Yes, baker. Tattenai's crew asks, “What are the names of the men who are constructing this building?” (Ezra 5:4) They want to know who's doing the work. Not just the work, the workers.
I can see why you'd guess that, but pay never comes up. The crew asks, “What are the names of the men who are constructing this building?” (Ezra 5:4) It's about who the men are, not what they earn.
Nobody asks to see a single hammer, friend. Tattenai's crew asks, “What are the names of the men who are constructing this building?” (Ezra 5:4) They want the men's names, not their equipment.

That's a natural guess when a governor shows up with questions. But the text says the elders “were not stopped until a report was sent to Darius and written instructions about this matter were returned.” (Ezra 5:5) The governor came with questions, not a stop sign. The work kept going while the answer was on its way.

That's right, baker. The text says the elders “were not stopped until a report was sent to Darius and written instructions about this matter were returned.” (Ezra 5:5) The governor asked his questions, and the work went on. A governor on the site, and the building doesn't even pause.
That's right. “…the eye of their God was on the elders of the Jews…” (Ezra 5:5) That's why they weren't stopped. The text doesn't say anything fancy about how, only that His eye was on them.

Cyrus, the king who issued the decree to rebuild (Ezra 5:13), does matter later in this story. But the text says whose eye was on the elders, and it isn't his. “…the eye of their God was on the elders of the Jews…” (Ezra 5:5) That's the reason they weren't stopped.

Haggai is one of the prophets who prophesied to the Jews, and the prophets were with the builders, helping them. (Ezra 5:1-2) But the eye on the elders belongs to someone else. “…the eye of their God was on the elders of the Jews…” (Ezra 5:5)

Baker, that's right. Tattenai tells King Darius, “This work is being carried out diligently and is prospering in their hands.” (Ezra 5:8) He's the one asking all the questions, and he still writes that down. The man came to question the builders and ended up writing them a glowing report.

You might expect a governor to run down the builders, but he doesn't. Tattenai writes to the king, “This work is being carried out diligently and is prospering in their hands.” (Ezra 5:8) So the letter says the work is going well. Good news, delivered by the man with the questions.

explanations.answer: Servants of the God of heaven and earth
explanations.explanation: Yes, baker. The elders answer, “We are servants of the God of heaven and earth…” (Ezra 5:11) A governor asks who they answer to, and they say it first thing. Not a title, not a name drop, just who they serve.

explanations.answer: Servants of the great King Darius
explanations.explanation: Darius is the king of Persia, the one Tattenai is writing to, so it's an understandable guess. But the elders never call themselves his servants. They say, “We are servants of the God of heaven and earth…” (Ezra 5:11)

explanations.answer: Servants of the governor of Judah
explanations.explanation: Nobody in this passage gets called that. When Tattenai asks who they are, the elders answer, “We are servants of the God of heaven and earth…” (Ezra 5:11) Standing in front of a governor, they name a higher boss.

That's it, baker. The elders say they're rebuilding the temple “…a great king of Israel built and completed.” (Ezra 5:11) The text doesn't name him here. The point is it was a real temple with a real history, and they weren't starting from nothing.

Prophets matter a lot in this story, since Haggai and Zechariah just spoke to the people. (Ezra 5:1) But the elders say, “…a great king of Israel built and completed.” (Ezra 5:11) So the builder of that first temple is called a king.
Jeshua is a priest in this story, so it's a fair guess. But the elders don't call the builder that. They say it was “…a great king of Israel built and completed.” (Ezra 5:11)

explanations.answer: Their fathers angered the God of heaven
explanations.explanation: That's right, baker. The elders say, “…since our fathers angered the God of heaven, He delivered them into the hand of Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon…” (Ezra 5:12) Nebuchadnezzar is the Chaldean who destroyed the temple. I think it takes some guts to say that out loud to a governor, but the elders say it plainly.

explanations.answer: Their fathers left the temple unfinished
explanations.explanation: The text doesn't give that reason. The elders say, “…since our fathers angered the God of heaven, He delivered them into the hand of Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon…” (Ezra 5:12) That's the only reason they give for what happened.

explanations.answer: Their fathers moved God's house elsewhere
explanations.explanation: Nothing in the elders' answer says that. They say, “…since our fathers angered the God of heaven, He delivered them into the hand of Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon…” (Ezra 5:12) Nebuchadnezzar was the king of Babylon who destroyed the temple. So the reason is that the fathers angered God.

Yes, baker. The elders say, “In the first year of his reign, however, Cyrus king of Babylon issued a decree to rebuild this house of God.” (Ezra 5:13) That little word “however” is where the story turns. After the hard part comes the hopeful part.

Darius is the king reading Tattenai's letter, so he's on everybody's mind. But the elders point back to an earlier king. “In the first year of his reign, however, Cyrus king of Babylon issued a decree to rebuild this house of God.” (Ezra 5:13)

That name doesn't show up anywhere in this passage. The elders say, “In the first year of his reign, however, Cyrus king of Babylon issued a decree to rebuild this house of God.” (Ezra 5:13) It's Cyrus who gave the decree.

You got it, baker. Cyrus gave the gold and silver articles “to a man named Sheshbazzar, whom he appointed governor…” (Ezra 5:14) A governor's job and a pile of gold and silver, all in one handoff. That's a big day for Sheshbazzar.
That name doesn't appear in this passage. The elders say Cyrus gave the articles “to a man named Sheshbazzar, whom he appointed governor…” (Ezra 5:14) So Sheshbazzar is the one who got the job.

Nehemiah isn't named anywhere in this passage. The elders tell Tattenai that Cyrus gave the articles “to a man named Sheshbazzar, whom he appointed governor…” (Ezra 5:14) That's the name to remember here.

Yes, baker. The elders quote Cyrus telling Sheshbazzar, “Take these articles, put them in the temple in Jerusalem, and let the house of God be rebuilt on its original site.” (Ezra 5:15) Same site, the very same spot. The instructions were clear.

It does say that. The elders quote Cyrus telling Sheshbazzar, “Take these articles, put them in the temple in Jerusalem, and let the house of God be rebuilt on its original site.” (Ezra 5:15) So the rebuilding goes on the original site, no moving the building anywhere else.

That's right. The elders say Sheshbazzar “came and laid the foundation of the house of God in Jerusalem…” (Ezra 5:16) That's where it all started. A building has to begin somewhere, and this one began at the bottom.

A roof is a fun guess, but it's not what the elders say. Sheshbazzar “came and laid the foundation of the house of God in Jerusalem…” (Ezra 5:16) The elders add that the work has been under construction since then and isn't completed. So the foundation is the starting point.
Doors aren't mentioned in this part of the story. The elders say Sheshbazzar “came and laid the foundation of the house of God in Jerusalem…” (Ezra 5:16) The foundation is the part he laid.

That's an easy mix-up, since they've been building a long time. But the elders say, “…from that time until now it has been under construction, but it has not yet been completed.” (Ezra 5:16) They're straight with the governor about where things stand. No ribbon cutting yet.

That's right, baker. The elders say, “…from that time until now it has been under construction, but it has not yet been completed.” (Ezra 5:16) The work has been going since the foundation was laid, and it's still in progress. They don't oversell it to the governor.

Yes, baker. Tattenai writes, “…let a search be made of the royal archives in Babylon to see if King Cyrus did indeed issue a decree to rebuild the house of God in Jerusalem.” (Ezra 5:17) He wants it checked in the records. Somebody's about to get stuck with a dusty job.

Palaces sound royal, but the letter doesn't ask for those. Tattenai writes, “…let a search be made of the royal archives in Babylon…” (Ezra 5:17) The search is for old records, not a tour of the king's houses.
Good guess for a governor's letter, but it's not the word. Tattenai writes, “…let a search be made of the royal archives in Babylon…” (Ezra 5:17) The decree would be found in the records.
